Duties include water supply, wastewater, and flood control engineering; US wages and employment use the 17-2051 civil engineers parent occupation as a proxy, and the parent occupation headcount is not labeled as the water treatment engineer headcount.

Inputs include water quantity and quality, site and pipe network data, applicable standards, service demand, costs, and operating constraints. First verify the source, sampling time, units, and range of variation; a single concentration cannot support a complete treatment design.

Tasks may include water quality studies, treatment method comparison, facility and equipment selection, pump station and pipe network design, and hydraulic analysis. Carry out professional analysis according to the position's division of work; implementable process parameters cannot be obtained directly from an occupational description.

Outputs include options, drawings, calculations and model descriptions, feasibility and cost-benefit analysis, environmental documents, and technical reports. Assumptions, data versions, review comments, and responsible persons must be traceable, and reports should not conceal unconfirmed conditions.

Process design focuses on pollutants and treatment methods; pipe network hydraulics focuses on flow, pressure loss, and facility connections. The two collaborate on projects, and whether one position covers both depends on the organization and project scope.

Collaborates with design and CAD technicians, owners, operations, and the engineering team, providing technical guidance and reviewing options. Owner requirements, construction conditions, operating feedback, and the responsible professional's confirmation are recorded separately.
